claims.text: AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 can be produced as dense bulk material by powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering.
The SPS-processed AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 alloy has a multiphase microstructure.
The selected AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 material is representative of a eutectic high-entropy alloy.
AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 naturally forms a coherent, protective oxide film at 600–700°C.
The oxide layer formed on AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 under elevated-temperature atmospheric wear improves wear resistance.
Cyclic mechanical abrasion physically disrupts the protective oxide film.
Repeated oxide-film disruption prevents the film from healing.
Abrasion-induced film disruption exposes fresh reactive metallic phases.
Exposure of the underlying metallic phases promotes aggressive localized corrosion.
Localized corrosion and passive-film breakdown compromise the film's protective capability.
Localized corrosion subsequently weakens the material's resistance to wear.
Static corrosion without abrasion allows formation and maintenance of a continuous protective oxide film.
The proposed comparison holds the chemical environment constant while applying cyclic wear only to the test group.
High-temperature electrochemical impedance spectroscopy can track oxide-film integrity during wear cycles.
Cyclically worn samples will have markedly higher total degradation than the static-corrosion baseline.
Cyclically worn samples will show greater corrosion-related metal loss and higher corrosion current density than the static-corrosion baseline.
Cyclically worn samples will exhibit higher wear rates because oxide-film support is lost.
The proposed mechanism is limited to oxidizing environments at 600–700°C in which a stable protective oxide normally exists.
The quantitative degradation response depends on abrasion intensity, oxide-healing rate, and the exact corrosive environment.
Observation of a continuous oxide film during cyclic wear together with no significant corrosion difference from the static control would falsify oxide disruption as the primary degradation driver.
